definition: A procedure with one observable result caused by exactly one substance: add the reagent, watch for the positive result, name the ion or gas it proves.
msAccepts: procedure whose positive result identifies a specific ion or gas
reagent + observation + conclusion
msAvoids: calling any colour change a test without naming the reagent and the conclusion
tests that identify a whole compound at once

definition: A positive ion, formed when an atom loses electrons. Every salt contains at least one cation and one anion; the flame test and sodium hydroxide tests identify the cation.
msAccepts: positive ion
metal or ammonium ion attracted to the cathode in electrolysis
msAvoids: saying cations gain electrons
confusing the charge with the flame colour

definition: A negative ion, formed when an atom gains electrons. Chloride, bromide, iodide, sulfate and carbonate are the anions tested with acid-plus-reagent scripts.
msAccepts: negative ion
non-metal ion tested by precipitation or gas-evolution reactions
msAvoids: saying anions lose electrons
calling the halide test a cation test

definition: Calcium hydroxide solution, Ca(OH)₂(aq) — an alkali. Turns milky with carbon dioxide because insoluble calcium carbonate precipitates.
msAccepts: calcium hydroxide solution
reagent in the carbon dioxide test giving a white precipitate of CaCO₃
msAvoids: confusing limewater with lime juice or plain water
saying limewater turns CO₂ milky — the limewater is what turns milky

definition: The HCO₃⁻ ion. Calcium hydrogencarbonate, Ca(HCO₃)₂, is soluble — which is why continued bubbling of CO₂ dissolves the white calcium carbonate precipitate.
msAccepts: soluble product formed when excess CO₂ reacts with calcium carbonate
explains the milkiness disappearing
msAvoids: calling it hydrogen carbonate inconsistently — one name per answer
saying the precipitate evaporates

definition: To strip the colour from a substance chemically. Chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper white; the dye is destroyed, not flipped to the other colour.
msAccepts: chlorine turns damp litmus white by destroying the dye
a chemical decolourising, distinct from an indicator colour flip
msAvoids: calling the red-to-white change an acid-base indicator result
saying dry litmus bleaches as readily

definition: A soluble base; a source of hydroxide ions in water. Ammonia is the only alkaline gas on the course — it turns damp red litmus blue.
msAccepts: ammonia identified as the only alkaline gas at this level
gas turning damp red litmus or universal indicator paper blue
msAvoids: calling chlorine alkaline — its solution is acidic then bleaching
forgetting the paper must be damp

definition: Containing no water of crystallisation. Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate is a white powder that turns blue when water is added to it.
msAccepts: white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate as the water-presence test reagent
without water of crystallisation
msAvoids: saying anhydrous means dry of all liquid generally — the term is about crystallisation water
reversing the colour change (white to blue on adding water)

definition: Water molecules built into a crystal's structure in fixed ratio — CuSO₄·5H₂O. Removing it leaves the anhydrous salt; restoring it turns the white solid blue.
msAccepts: water molecules in fixed ratio within the crystal lattice
anhydrous copper(II) sulfate regaining it and turning blue
msAvoids: saying the crystals are merely wet
writing the dot formula without the ratio

definition: Containing water of crystallisation — hydrated copper(II) sulfate is CuSO₄·5H₂O and is blue, the colour the water test produces.
msAccepts: blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate as the product of the water test
salt plus water of crystallisation
msAvoids: confusing hydrated with simply containing liquid water
omitting the 5H₂O ratio in the formula

definition: Cation test: dip a platinum or nichrome wire in concentrated hydrochloric acid, then the sample salt, hold in a non-luminous flame, read the colour.
msAccepts: acid-cleaned wire, sample, non-luminous flame, colour read as the cation
identifies metal ions by their emission colour
msAvoids: omitting the wire cleaning
using the yellow luminous flame, whose colour drowns the result

definition: The blue roaring Bunsen flame with the air hole open. Used for flame tests because it adds no colour of its own; the yellow safety flame would.
msAccepts: air hole open, blue roaring flame
chosen so the flame itself contributes no colour
msAvoids: calling it the safety flame
saying the yellow flame is used because it is brighter

definition: An insoluble solid formed in a solution reaction; the solution goes cloudy. Precipitate colour is the evidence in the sodium hydroxide and silver nitrate tests.
msAccepts: insoluble solid formed when two solutions react
colour of the precipitate identifies the ion
msAvoids: calling any solid a precipitate — solids present before the reaction are not
testing on a solid sample where the precipitate would be invisible

definition: An equation showing only the species that actually react — for example Fe³⁺(aq) + 3OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₃(s). Preferred for precipitation reactions.
msAccepts: spectator ions omitted
charges and state symbols included
msAvoids: omitting the charges on aqueous ions
writing the full equation when the ionic one is asked for

definition: Does not dissolve in water. Most metal hydroxides are insoluble — the fact that makes the sodium hydroxide cation tests produce precipitates.
msAccepts: metal hydroxide precipitates because the hydroxide is insoluble
silver and barium halides/sulfates of the anion tests
msAvoids: saying 'not very soluble' when the mark wants insoluble
confusing insoluble with immiscible

definition: NH₄⁺ — the positive ion formed by ammonia accepting a proton. Sodium hydroxide releases ammonia gas from it: NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O.
msAccepts: ammonia gas evolved with NaOH, identified on damp red litmus
the proton-transfer from NH₄⁺ to OH⁻
msAvoids: writing NH₃ for the ammonium ion — the ion has four hydrogens and a positive charge
expecting a precipitate — ammonium hydroxide is not insoluble

definition: The CO₃²⁻ ion. Fizzes with dilute hydrochloric acid giving CO₂, confirmed by limewater turning milky; most carbonates are insoluble solids.
msAccepts: acid + fizzing + limewater confirmation identifies a carbonate
CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → CO₂ + H₂O as the general ionic equation
msAvoids: claiming fizzing alone proves carbonate — metals fizz with hydrogen
forgetting the limewater confirmation half

definition: The SO₄²⁻ ion. Identified by adding dilute hydrochloric acid then barium chloride solution — a white precipitate of barium sulfate, BaSO₄.
msAccepts: acid first then barium chloride, white precipitate
sulfuric acid banned because it carries sulfate ions itself
msAvoids: omitting the acid-first interference-removal step
acidifying with sulfuric acid in this test

definition: The −1 ions of Group 7: chloride, bromide, iodide. Acidify with nitric acid, add silver nitrate: AgCl white, AgBr cream, AgI yellow.
msAccepts: Group 7 −1 ions named collectively as halides
the three silver halide colours in specification words
msAvoids: including fluoride in the tested set — only Cl/Br/I are examined
acidifying with any hydrohalic acid, which adds halide ions of its own

definition: Made acidic before the reagent is added — dilute nitric acid for the halide test, dilute hydrochloric acid for the sulfate test, always before the precipitating reagent.
msAccepts: acid added before the reagent to remove interfering anions
nitric acid chosen for halide tests because nitrates stay soluble
msAvoids: swapping the acid and reagent order
using an acid whose anion is the ion under test
